description: Power Receiver Controller 1C QFN-16L-EP(3x3) Power Management - Specialized

provenance.pins: datasheet p.4-5 Table 1 Pin Function Descriptions; limits p.9 Table 4 ABSOLUTE MAXIMUM RATINGS

notes: FIGURE 6 RESOLVED (source: https://www.hynetek.com/2730.html, found by research, NOT in the datasheet). The unlabelled 'Voltage Regulator' is a BSS138 source follower: gate via 10 kOhm pull-up clamped by a 28 V Zener, source to the VBUS pin. A 0 Ohm link bypasses it at 28 V and below.

THE GATE DRIVE NEEDS A SEPARATE FIX THAT FIGURE 6 DOES NOT SHOW. Figures 4, 5 and 6 all draw the SAME Zener gate network - it is not a 48 V feature. Above 28 V Hynetek replaces it: GATE pulled to the MCU's 3V3 through 5.1 kOhm, level-shifted through a PMOS-then-NMOS pair into the high-side P-FET, clamped by a 15 V Zener and 100 kOhm. Reading Figure 6 alone and copying its gate network would be wrong at 36 V.

NO OVERVOLTAGE PROTECTION ABOVE 28 V. Hynetek states it directly: '因为HUSB238A没有36V/48V OV保护'. The clamp preserves the supply function and VBUS-present detection but destroys OVP, UVP and the discharge path. This is also why 48 V is I2C-only while GPIO mode stops at 28 V. Accepted consequence of the topology, not a mistake to design around - but it means the bus TVS and our own ADC sense are the only overvoltage protection the system has.

INDUSTRY CONTEXT: this clamp approach is the outlier. The common solution is an active 0.42x ratiometric level shifter in a companion IC (TI TPD4S480, Kinetic KTU1133, Fortune FA2218), which PRESERVES measurement where Hynetek's clamp does not.

VBUS PIN LIMIT IS NOT THE SYSTEM LIMIT. The pin is 3.15-29.4 V recommended, 33 V absolute (p.6 Table 2, p.9 Table 4), but the chip supports up to 48 V/5 A at the SYSTEM level. Figure 6 on p.16, 'HUSB238A configured as I2C mode (Maximum 48V)', shows how: VBUS reaches the chip's VBUS pin through an external VOLTAGE REGULATOR that drops it into range, while the high-voltage bus passes through an external P-FET driven by GATE (this design does not use that path - see README), with a Zener clamping the gate network to protect the 33 V GATE pin. Figures 4 and 5 on p.15 are the 28 V variants; p.16 is easy to miss because the schematic is a pure image with no extractable text.

EPR fixed PDOs are 28 V, 36 V and 48 V. Which one to request is a SYSTEM decision set by the load: the XL1509 on the LED modules is 4.5-40 V operating / 45 V absolute, so 48 V would destroy them. 36 V x 5 A = 180 W is the highest usable option.
Pin 17 is the exposed thermal pad and is GND. It must be connected.
ADDR pin 8 selects the mode at power-up: tied to VDD = I2C addr 0x62, to GND = I2C addr 0x42, floating = GPIO mode. Use a 900k resistor when tying, to keep standby current low.
GPIO mode caps at 28 V/3.25 A (91 W). I2C mode is required for 5 A.
VDD can be left unpowered: the chip self-powers from VBUS (pin 16) when VDD is absent, so it negotiates before any downstream rail exists.
D+/D- (pins 1-2) are for legacy protocol detection (BC1.2, QC2.0, HVDCP) only. PD itself runs on CC1/CC2, so they can be left unconnected if only PD is needed.

rules.note: datasheet p.4: place a 1uF ceramic across VDD and GND
pin 17 is the exposed pad and the only GND connection
datasheet p.5: INT_N is open-drain and needs a pull-up to be readable

Above 28 V the VBUS pin must sit behind the p.16 Figure 6 BSS138 source follower - never tied straight to a 36 V bus. GATE is deliberately left unconnected in this design: there is no external VBUS switch for it to drive. See the design README's Gate network section.
